body:
What does a diagnostic test identify?

A diagnostic test provides information that helps determine whether a disease or condition is present. Different tests examine different biological substances. Some identify genetic material from an organism, while others detect proteins, antigens, antibodies or changes in the patient's own cells.

A test result is evidence used in clinical assessment. It must be interpreted with the patient's symptoms, exposure history, timing of sample collection and other relevant findings.

PCR: Detecting specific DNA sequences

Polymerase chain reaction (PCR) is a technique used to make many copies of a selected DNA region. The increase in copies is called amplification.

Amplification is useful because a biological sample may contain only a small amount of the target DNA. By increasing the detectable quantity of a selected region, PCR can help identify an organism or genetic variation that might otherwise be difficult to detect.

For example, a PCR-based test may look for a DNA sequence characteristic of a particular pathogen. A different assay may look for a specified genetic change associated with a disease.

Molecular diagnostic test: A test that examines biological molecules, especially DNA or RNA, to help identify a pathogen, a genetic variation or another disease-related feature.

RT-PCR: When the target is RNA

Some viruses have RNA as their genetic material. Conventional PCR amplifies DNA rather than RNA. Therefore, an RNA target can first be converted into complementary DNA using an enzyme called reverse transcriptase. PCR can then amplify the resulting DNA.

This approach is called reverse transcription PCR, commonly abbreviated RT-PCR. It is used in molecular testing for several RNA viruses.

The term real-time PCR refers to measurement of amplification during the reaction. Reverse transcription and real-time detection are different concepts, although they may be combined in one assay.

PCR: Amplifies DNA. Reverse transcription PCR: Converts an RNA target into DNA before amplification. Real-time PCR: Monitors amplification as it occurs. Do not assume that reverse transcription and real-time detection mean the same thing.

Antigen and antibody tests detect different targets

An antigen test detects a selected antigen, often a protein associated with a pathogen. It does not necessarily amplify genetic material. Some antigen tests are designed to give rapid results, but their sensitivity can differ from that of molecular tests.

An antibody test looks for antibodies produced by the patient's immune system. Antibodies may become detectable only after sufficient time has passed for an immune response to develop. Depending on the disease and test, a positive antibody result may reflect current infection, previous infection or vaccination.

Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA) uses the specific interaction between an antigen and an antibody to produce a measurable result. Different ELISA formats can detect either an antigen or an antibody.

What common tests detect

Test or approachMain targetImportant interpretation
PCRSelected DNA sequenceDetects target genetic material after amplification
Reverse transcription PCRRNA target, converted into DNAUseful for detecting selected RNA sequences
Antigen testSpecific antigen, often a proteinEvidence that the tested antigen is present
Antibody testAntibodies made by the patientMay indicate an immune response to infection or vaccination
ELISAAntigen or antibody, according to the assayUses antigen-antibody binding for detection
DNA sequencingOrder of bases in selected DNA or broader DNA regionsCan identify genetic variations; interpretation depends on the purpose and scope

PCR and sequencing are not identical

PCR usually focuses on amplifying a selected DNA region. DNA sequencing determines the order of nucleotide bases in the material being examined. Sequencing may cover a small region, a collection of genes or much larger parts of a genome.

For many clinical questions, a targeted molecular test is sufficient. Reading an entire genome is not automatically necessary or better.

Understanding sensitivity and specificity

Sensitivity describes a test's ability to identify people who truly have the condition under the circumstances in which it is evaluated. A test with higher sensitivity generally produces fewer false-negative results.

Specificity describes a test's ability to identify people who do not have the condition. A test with higher specificity generally produces fewer false-positive results.

Neither measure means that a test is infallible. Test performance also depends on sample quality, timing and correct use.

Why a positive molecular test needs interpretation

Detection of genetic material does not always prove that a living, infectious organism remains present. Some tests may detect residual genetic material after an infection has resolved. Similarly, a negative result can occur when the tested substance is absent from the particular sample or present below the detection limit.

The probability that a positive result represents a true case also depends on how common the disease is in the population being tested. This is why screening and diagnosis require clinical context.

Prelims focus

  • PCR amplifies selected DNA sequences.
  • Reverse transcriptase converts RNA into complementary DNA.
  • Antigen tests detect antigens; antibody tests detect the body's immune response.
  • ELISA is based on antigen-antibody interaction.
  • Higher sensitivity generally reduces false negatives; higher specificity generally reduces false positives.
  • Trap: Detection of pathogen genetic material does not always establish that the patient remains infectious.

[NCERT, Biology, Class XII, Chapter 11, Biotechnology: Principles and Processes, section 11.3.3, Amplification of Gene of Interest Using PCR; Chapter 12, Biotechnology and Its Applications, section 12.2.3, Molecular Diagnosis; US National Library of Medicine, MedlinePlus, PCR Tests, sections on purpose and interpretation; US Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, respiratory-virus testing guidance, sections on molecular and antigen tests, consulted 13 November 2026.]

body:
What is a biomarker?

A biomarker is a measurable biological characteristic that provides information about a normal process, a disease process or the body's response to an exposure or treatment.

Biomarkers are not limited to genes. They may include a protein concentration, an enzyme level, a hormone, a genetic variation or another measurable biological feature.

For example, blood glucose concentration is a measurable indicator used in the assessment and management of diabetes. The HER2 protein status of a tumour can help identify patients who may benefit from particular targeted cancer treatments.

Biomarkers serve different purposes

Biomarker roleQuestion answeredIllustration
DiagnosticDoes the evidence support the presence of a condition?A disease-associated molecular finding
PredictiveIs a particular treatment more likely to benefit this patient?HER2 status when considering HER2-directed therapy
PrognosticWhat does a finding suggest about the likely course of disease?A validated disease-risk marker
MonitoringHow is the condition changing over time?Repeated blood glucose measurements during diabetes management

The same biological measurement may have more than one use. Its role depends on the clinical question and whether the test has been validated for that purpose.

Meaning of precision medicine

Precision medicine uses relevant differences among patients to help select prevention, diagnostic or treatment approaches. These differences may include age, disease characteristics, biomarkers, genetic information and other clinical findings.

Traditional treatment often begins with an approach that works for many people with the same diagnosis. Precision medicine adds further information to help determine which option is most appropriate for a particular group of patients.

Precision medicine: An approach that uses clinical, molecular, genomic and other relevant information to guide prevention, diagnosis or treatment while accounting for differences among patients.

Precision medicine is not the same as producing a separate medicine for every individual. Often the practical result is selecting an existing treatment for the group of patients most likely to benefit from it.

How a biomarker can guide targeted treatment

Consider a patient diagnosed with breast cancer. The diagnosis identifies the disease, but the tumour's biological features can provide additional information. If testing shows HER2 positivity under appropriate clinical criteria, a HER2-targeting medicine such as trastuzumab may be considered.

The biomarker helps determine treatment suitability. It does not guarantee success, and a negative result for one target does not mean that no effective treatment exists.

Inherited genetic changes and changes arising in a tumour

Genetic tests can investigate different sources of variation.

  • Germline variation: A genetic variation that can be passed to offspring through egg or sperm cells. It can be relevant to inherited disease susceptibility and may have implications for biological relatives.
  • Somatic variation: A genetic change arising in particular cells during a person's life. A change found in a tumour may help explain its behaviour or indicate a possible treatment target.

A tumour-specific genetic finding is not automatically inherited by the patient's children. Likewise, finding an inherited risk variation does not prove that the person currently has the disease.

Screening, diagnosis and treatment selection

Screening looks for evidence of disease or risk in people who may not have symptoms. Diagnosis determines whether a disease is present using appropriate evidence. Treatment selection uses information about an established condition to choose suitable care.

One test may be useful for screening but insufficient for a final diagnosis. Another test may be important only after a diagnosis has been established. The purpose of the test must therefore be understood before interpreting its result.

Limits of precision medicine

Biological differences among patients are important, but not every disease can be explained by one gene or biomarker. Environmental exposures, other illnesses, age, nutrition, behaviour and access to healthcare may also affect outcomes.

A biomarker must demonstrate clinical usefulness before it becomes a reliable basis for treatment decisions. A newly discovered association does not automatically justify widespread testing.

Prelims focus

  • A biomarker is a measurable biological characteristic; it need not be genetic.
  • A predictive biomarker helps estimate suitability for a particular treatment.
  • HER2 status can guide consideration of HER2-directed treatment.
  • Germline changes can be passed to offspring; somatic changes arise in particular cells during life.
  • Screening, diagnosis and treatment selection are different clinical purposes.
  • Trap: Precision medicine does not mean gene editing or creating a unique drug for every patient.

[US National Cancer Institute, Biomarker Testing for Cancer Treatment, sections on what biomarkers are and how testing guides treatment; US National Cancer Institute, Trastuzumab, Drug Information Summary; World Health Organization, World Health Assembly endorses resolution on precision medicine, 22 May 2026, definition and policy objectives, consulted 13 November 2026.]

title: Biomarkers and Precision Medicine: Using Test Results to Guide Care

body:
Why the same medicine can affect people differently

Two patients may receive the same medicine yet experience different benefits or adverse effects. These differences can arise from age, body functions, other medicines, disease severity, lifestyle and genetic variation.

Some genes influence the production or activity of enzymes that process medicines. Other genes affect how drugs move through the body or how tissues respond to them.

Pharmacogenomics studies how genetic variation can influence a person's response to medicines. Its practical purpose is to support safer and more effective selection of treatment when there is sufficient clinical evidence.

Pharmacogenomics: The study of how differences in genetic information influence drug effectiveness, drug processing or the risk of adverse reactions.

Drug processing and the role of enzymes

After administration, many drugs are absorbed, distributed, chemically changed and eventually eliminated. The liver contains several enzymes that participate in drug metabolism.

Genetic variations can influence how efficiently a particular enzyme works. However, reduced enzyme activity does not have the same effect on every medicine.

For a drug that must be broken down to be removed, slower metabolism may cause higher drug concentrations. For a prodrug that must be converted into an active medicine, slower metabolism may instead reduce the amount of active drug produced.

The CYP2C19 and clopidogrel example

Clopidogrel is an antiplatelet medicine that helps reduce the formation of harmful blood clots in certain patients. It is a prodrug, meaning that the administered substance must undergo metabolic activation before it produces its main intended effect.

The enzyme system involving CYP2C19 contributes to this activation. Some inherited variations reduce CYP2C19 function.

Patients classified as CYP2C19 intermediate or poor metabolisers may form lower amounts of clopidogrel's active metabolite and have a weaker antiplatelet response. This may be associated with increased cardiovascular risk in relevant clinical situations.

The effect of reduced enzyme activity depends on the drug. It is incorrect to conclude that a poor metaboliser must always experience increased drug action. Clopidogrel illustrates the opposite possibility because it requires activation.

Genetic variations can also influence drug safety

Pharmacogenomics is not limited to determining how quickly a medicine is metabolised. Some genetic markers are associated with a greater likelihood of serious adverse reactions.

For example, the HLA-B*57:01 genetic marker is associated with an increased risk of a serious hypersensitivity reaction to the medicine abacavir. This is an example of genetic information helping identify an important treatment-related risk.

The relevant clinical recommendations depend on the medicine and the supporting evidence. A pharmacogenomic result must therefore be interpreted using reliable clinical guidance rather than general assumptions about genes.

Does every patient need genetic testing before receiving medicines?

No. Pharmacogenomic testing is useful only when the result can provide relevant and sufficiently reliable information for a particular treatment decision.

Many medicines can be prescribed safely without genetic testing. For others, clinical factors, laboratory findings or monitoring may be more useful than genetic information alone.

Even when a gene-drug association is well established, the result does not replace clinical judgement. Kidney and liver function, other medicines, allergies and the patient's condition may still affect the choice or dose of treatment.

Pharmacogenomics and precision medicine

Pharmacogenomics is one application of precision medicine. It focuses on differences in drug response, whereas precision medicine covers a wider set of decisions involving diagnosis, prevention and treatment.

A genetic test that identifies a drug-processing variation is therefore different from a test used to detect the DNA of an infectious organism. Both may use molecular technology, but they answer different questions.

Prelims focus

  • Pharmacogenomics connects genetic variation with drug response.
  • CYP2C19 contributes to the activation of clopidogrel.
  • Reduced CYP2C19 function may produce less active clopidogrel and a weaker antiplatelet effect.
  • HLA-B*57:01 is associated with abacavir hypersensitivity risk.
  • Genetic information is only one factor in prescribing decisions.
  • Trap: Slower drug metabolism does not always mean a stronger drug effect; the result depends on whether metabolism activates or removes the drug.

[US Food and Drug Administration, Table of Pharmacogenetic Associations, section 1, entries for Clopidogrel–CYP2C19 and Abacavir–HLA-B*57:01, consulted 13 November 2026; National Human Genome Research Institute, Pharmacogenomics, Genetics Glossary, consulted 13 November 2026; World Health Organization, World Health Assembly endorses resolution on precision medicine, 22 May 2026.]
